fatal_errors: The hypothesis concerns hierarchical HfNbTiVAl10, whereas the target study designed an as-cast Nb-Mo-Ta-V-W alloy from an equimolar NbMoTaVW baseline.

It replaces the target intervention—rule-of-mixtures modulus validation followed by screening 38,326 compositions using modulus, VEC, and density—with an unvalidated imaging/ML/reduced-order simulation framework.
It proposes tensile and fracture-toughness prediction, while the decisive target experiment was room-temperature quasi-static compression and did not report fracture toughness.
It omits the selected Nb15Mo2.5Ta40V40W2.5 composition, reduced-VEC design rationale, single-phase BCC structure, and Peierls-barrier/dislocation-mobility mechanism.
The claimed 10% accuracy and 10-fold efficiency gains are not supported by the cited evidence.

The cited evidence supports only broad applicability of machine learning to alloy-property prediction; it does not validate microstructure-image descriptors, toughness prediction, or the proposed efficiency gain.
explanation: The generated proposal is a testable alternative methodology, but it does not reconstruct the hidden study in material system, baseline, intervention, test mode, mechanism, or outcome. The target used inexpensive composition-based screening and selected Nb15Mo2.5Ta40V40W2.5 for low VEC with retained modulus, then demonstrated 35.7 ± 0.9% compressive fracture strain, 1115 ± 18 MPa yield strength, and 2550 ± 75 MPa compressive strength. None of these central elements appears in the hypothesis. Its blinded benchmark provides some discriminability, but it lacks a specified sample count, controlled microstructural variation, toughness standard, uncertainty treatment, and comparison protocol. Its out-of-distribution caveats are reasonable in general, yet the 800 °C threshold is arbitrary and does not capture the target model's actual limitation: omission of grain size, phases, defects, and processing history.
